new.title: Visit Father Damien's tomb in the Sint-Antoniuskapel
new.desc: Jozef De Veuster, the Picpus missionary known as Father Damien of Hawaii, lies in the crypt of this small chapel. His remains were brought back from Hawaii in 1936 in the presence of King Leopold III, and he was declared a saint in 2009.
new.tip: The chapel stands on Pater Damiaanplein, a few minutes south of the Oude Markt. The crypt is downstairs, below the chapel itself.

new.title: Cycle out to Vlierbeek Abbey in Kessel-Lo
new.desc: Benedictines from Affligem settled here in 1127 and the priory became an abbey in the 1160s. The neoclassical church was designed by Laurent-Benoît Dewez and built from 1776, and it still serves as the parish church of Vlierbeek.
new.tip: The church is open outside service times and there is a tavern on the grounds. The other abbey buildings are lived in, so keep to the paths.

new.title: Graze the Friday market around the university library
new.desc: Every Friday Leuven's weekly market spreads over Monseigneur Ladeuzeplein and Herbert Hooverplein, in the shadow of the library tower. It is where locals stock up for the weekend and pick up something to eat on the spot.
new.tip: Go in the morning for the best choice. On Saturdays another market in the centre adds cured meats, cheese, mushrooms and a few antiques.

new.title: Drink beer piped across the street at Domus
new.desc: Domus calls itself the first craft house brewery in the Benelux. Its beers run through a copper pipe from the small brewery across the street straight to the taps of the tavern, where they are served with traditional Flemish dishes.
new.tip: The brewery, with its medieval cellar, can be toured with a guide by groups of eight or more who book ahead. Everyone else can simply order the house beers at the bar.

new.title: Sip a taproom-only beer at De Coureur in Kessel-Lo
new.desc: Brewer Bart and his partner Ine run this microbrewery in Kessel-Lo and compare their beers to the riders who lead a bike race. Everything is brewed on site and served only in the taproom, so you will not find these beers anywhere else.
new.tip: The taproom opens on Wednesday to Friday evenings and from midday at the weekend, when there are also guided brewery tours. They make their own soft drinks too.

new.title: Picnic beside the old city wall in Sint-Donatuspark
new.desc: This small landscape park was laid out between 1869 and 1875, a few steps from Ladeuzeplein. Running through it is a fragment of Leuven's first city wall from the 12th century, with two of its towers, and there is a cast-iron bandstand of 1898.
new.tip: It is the handiest patch of grass in the centre for a picnic, and students fill it on warm days. The main gate once belonged to an old university college.

new.title: Climb the staircase to nowhere on the Vlooyberg
new.desc: On one of the highest hills of the Hageland, a rust-coloured steel staircase rises into thin air and simply stops. The Vlooybergtoren of 2013 is 11 metres high, 20 metres long and weighs 13 tonnes, and on a clear day the view reaches the cooling towers of Vilvoorde and the mine headframe of Beringen.
new.tip: Pick a clear day, since the view is the whole point. The tower stands in open country outside Tielt, so expect wind on the top step.

new.title: Go up the mended Maagdentoren in Zichem
new.desc: This round keep of brown ironstone was built around 1383, 26 metres high with walls four metres thick. A quarter of it collapsed in 2006 after decades of neglect, and the gap was closed with a modern section that holds a staircase to a viewing platform.
new.tip: From the stairs in the new section you can see just how thick the medieval walls are. Pair it with the basilica of Scherpenheuvel, a few kilometres away.

new.title: Stroll the Park van Hoegaarden behind the Kapittelhuis
new.desc: The Kapittelhuis beside the Sint-Gorgoniuskerk was once home to the canons of Hoegaarden. Its grounds became Flemish show gardens in 1991 and were reworked into the Park van Hoegaarden in 2021.
new.tip: Afterwards order the village's cloudy white beer, flavoured with coriander and orange peel. Pierre Celis brought the style back to life here in 1966.

new.title: Learn the story of the glass villages at Dru!f in Overijse
new.desc: The hills south-east of Brussels once held up to 35,000 greenhouses growing table grapes, which earned them the name of the glass villages. Dru!f, the visitor centre in the middle of Overijse, tells that story in an interactive exhibition and has its own café.
new.tip: Local table grapes are sold mainly from August to October, often straight from the few growers who are left. Check the opening hours with the town before you go.

new.title: Meet Holle Griet on the market square of Diest
new.desc: On the little square in front of Diest's old cloth hall sits Holle Griet, a medieval cannon made in 1465. A few steps away the Sint-Sulpitiuskerk, the town's main church, stands on the Grote Markt as a fine example of the local Demer Gothic style.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk on the green ramparts that still ring the town. The Lindenmolen windmill up there turns on the first Sunday of the month.

new.title: Taste bread, cheese and beer at Averbode Abbey
new.desc: The Norbertine abbey of Averbode, founded in 1134, puts its own products on the table at Het Moment in the abbey grounds. The bread and speculaas are baked in the house bakery and come with Averbode cheese and abbey beer in the café, with a shop alongside.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays. Park at the entrance on Herseltsebaan and leave time for a walk round the abbey grounds.

new.title: Order a Job at Brouwerij De Kroon in Neerijse
new.desc: In 2013 the family of Professor Freddy Delvaux, Belgium's leading beer flavour expert, opened a new brewery where an older village brewery once stood. Their beers, from Job to Superkroon, are poured in the bistro next door, right beside the Doode Bemde nature reserve.
new.tip: Brewery tours are by reservation only, but the bistro needs no planning. The bus from Leuven takes about twenty minutes.

new.title: Try Aarschotse Bruine at 't Bruine Café
new.desc: Aarschot's own brown beer died out when the last local brewer closed in 1969, until the town itself revived it in 1989. It is poured at 't Bruine Café, the mock old-time pub of the town museum, together with the town brewery's Forto and Duc.
new.tip: The café opens in the afternoon from Wednesday to Sunday. In summer take your glass out to the terrace in the museum garden.

new.title: Cross the boardwalks of Het Vinne in Zoutleeuw
new.desc: Het Vinne was once the largest natural lake in Flanders, until it was drained for farmland in the 1840s. The pumps were switched off in 2004 and the water came back, and today boardwalks cross the flooded hollow to a lookout tower at the water's edge.
new.tip: Bring binoculars: herons, ducks and geese are always about and rare terns have bred here. Galloway cattle graze the meadows.

new.title: Swim outdoors at the Halve Maan in Diest
new.desc: The provincial domain on the edge of Diest has one of the best-loved open-air pools in Flemish Brabant, with a sandy beach beside the water. The swimming season usually runs from the start of May to mid September.
new.tip: On hot days the pool can sell out, so sort out your ticket before setting off. People from Diest and from Flemish Brabant pay less than visitors from elsewhere.

new.title: Walk round the world in the Tervuren arboretum
new.desc: In 1902 botanist Charles Bommer laid out an arboretum on land belonging to King Leopold II in the Kapucijnenbos, part of the Sonian Forest. Its 120 hectares are divided into about a hundred sections by region of origin, so one walk takes you from western North America to the Mediterranean and the Far East.
new.tip: Autumn is the most colourful season, when the American and Asian sections turn. Paths are forest tracks, so wear proper shoes after rain.

new.title: Squelch along the log path in the Doode Bemde
new.desc: South of Leuven the Dijle runs through wet meadows that were never fit for farming, which is where the name comes from. Around 9 km of paths in two loops cross the reserve, including a log path over the wettest ground and two bird hides by the ponds.
new.tip: Start from the station of Sint-Joris-Weert or Oud-Heverlee, both within walking distance. Waterproof boots are a good idea for most of the year.
